 What we covered on election eve
 • Making their case: Senate candidates in races that could determine control of the chamber made their final pitches. From Michigan to Maine, Texas to Alaska, they outlined the stakes in contests that are also seen as a referendum on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term.
 • Trump’s message: The president closed out his midterm campaign blitz with a speech at the Reflecting Pool , where he held up photos touting his administration’s renovations. Earlier in the day, he said he would “veto everything” if Democrats win back power in Congress.
 • Top court weighs in: The Supreme Court quickly shut down Trump’s effort to force California to sideline potentially thousands of ballots that the Justice Department claims may have been cast by noncitizens, rejecting the administration’s emergency request hours after it was filed.

 Peltola celebrates "positive" campaign, urges Alaskans to get out and vote in final rally
 By Lex Harvey 
 Mary Peltola speaks to supporters during a campaign rally in Anchorage, Alaska on October 30. 
 Lindsey Wasson/AP 
 Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate, closed out her campaign on election eve, urging Alaskans to get out and vote.
 “It’s still a close race,” she said at a Monday evening rally in Fairbanks, urging her supporters to help their friends get to the polls. “If you have transportation, help somebody who doesn’t have a ride. Help somebody who is disabled. Help somebody who otherwise would not think of going, or would not have the wherewithal to go.”
 Peltola said her team has run “the best race Alaska has ever seen.”
 “We have kept this so positive,” she added. “We’ve kept this focused on Alaskans. We are not interested in smearing our friends and neighbors, and future colleagues.”
 In recent days, Peltola’s campaign has been marred by drama after the New York Times reported its alleged involvement in recruiting another man named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate to confuse voters. Peltola has denied she knew anything about the alleged scheme.
 In response, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay the certification of the race before the election was held. A federal judge threw out the lawsuit on Sunday.
 “They’re crying election interference as they’re interfering in an election,” Peltola said Monday. “We know hypocrisy when we see it.”

 'Very disappointed': Marjorie Taylor Greene on Trump's closing midterms message 
 2:07
 President Donald Trump focusing on the Reflecting Pool in his final speech before the midterms “was absolutely the wrong message,” former U.S. Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins tonight.
 “I was very disappointed, with Americans struggling with the continued rise of inflation that’s been going on since Covid, high prices with gas and diesel and constant complaining about the cost of health insurance and health care with no one listening to them — standing in front of the reflecting pool that most Americans, I would say 99.999% of Americans don’t ever think about on a daily basis was absolutely the wrong message to send to Americans, asking them to go vote for Republicans tomorrow,” she said.
 Greene, once an avid Trump supporter, fell out with the president last year, which also led her to resign from her seat as a Republican congresswoman in Georgia.
 Since the contentious breakup, Greene has been outspoken about some of Trump’s actions.
 Speaking with Collins, Greene said she has “no idea” why he chose to focus on that, and said he should’ve focused on the mandate Republicans were given in 2024 to “make life easier for Americans.”
 “However, the past two years haven’t been about that at all,” Greene said.

 "They are scared" Talarico says at Austin rally 
 0:11
 James Talarico closed his Democratic Senate race in Texas with a rally tonight in Austin, imploring a few thousand supporters to believe in the possibility of their power at the ballot box Tuesday.
 “Tomorrow night, we are going to do something extraordinary. We are going to do something historic,” Talarico said. “We are going to shock the nation, shock the world when we beat the billionaires and take back Texas.”
 It was the final stop on his 21-city “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour, a nod to the fabled Texas TV show “Friday Night Lights.”
 He spent one more night assailing Republican rival Ken Paxton and his biggest patron, Elon Musk, who has contributed more than $168 million to the campaign that has become the most expensive non-presidential race in the nation’s history.
 “They are scared. They are terrified,” Talarico said. “They see what we see: that we’re about to win this election tomorrow night.”
 “We are the underdogs,” he added. “We are literally going up against the richest man in the world.”
 “This election is a battle between the powers that be and the powers that ought to be.”

 Stevens defends GOP endorsement in lengthy post and denounces Democratic response
 By Danya Gainor 
 Less than 48 hours before Election Day, Rep. Haley Stevens ignited a Democratic firestorm in pulling her endorsement from her party’s Senate nominee in Michigan and backing Republican Mike Rogers. After Democrats took to publicly branding her a traitor, Stevens on Monday said that scrutiny has troubled her “almost as much” as the choice to break ranks in the first place.
 In a nearly 900-word post to X with the title “The Decisions We Make,” Stevens relived the fast-moving weekend spat, standing by her shocking decision to rescind her endorsement for Abdul El-Sayed and denounced the Democratic Party’s efforts to push her out .
 “Instead of asking why a lifelong Democrat reached this point, some leaders rushed to condemn me, question my motives, and push me out,” she wrote. “That response reveals something deeply troubling about what is missing in today’s Democratic Party.”
 She continued: “We cannot preach inclusion while punishing dissent. We cannot promise to heal a divided country if we cannot tolerate disagreement among ourselves. And we cannot build a lasting majority by making Americans feel their concerns are unwelcome.”
 The Michigan Democrat had posted her endorsement reversal to X on Sunday morning — racking up 29 million views — but did not post again on the platform until Monday night, the eve of a nail-biting Election Day. In the interim, she sat for a combative interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper Sunday evening, where she struggled to articulate why she changed her mind.
 “Loyalty to a party should never require abandoning your values or judgment,” she wrote Monday. “We can build a stronger, more welcoming, more courageous Democratic Party.”
 Signing off, Stevens wrote, “I plan to help lead that effort.”

 Trump makes final midterm push in a series of telerallies
 By Alejandra Jaramillo and Molly English 
 With no “God made Trump” video to introduce him, and no clip of CNN’s Harry Enten walking through the polls — across several telerallies on the eve of the midterm elections — President Donald Trump mostly stuck to the message he’s delivered at dozens of in-person rallies around the country: “Pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
 Trump started the day campaigning by phone for candidates in North Carolina. Then calling into virtual rallies in New York, South Carolina, Alaska, Georgia, Indiana, Louisiana and twice in Texas.
 The calls mostly played out as a much shorter version of the familiar in-person rally script. Trump insisted Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, said he is on the ballot and declared that “we’re in the golden age of America, and we’re not going to let” Democrats “rip it down.”
 Even as he stumped for other Republicans, much of the focus stayed on Trump himself.
 “At least you like me, but I think you love me,” Trump told GOP Senate candidate Darline Graham in South Carolina.
 In Alaska, he went after Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola after a report alleged her campaign helped recruit a second Dan Sullivan to run against GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
 His choice to pivot to telerallies on the eve of the election came after hosting nearly 30 in-person rallies in mostly red states across the country is one that has confounded some. Plans for in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas this past weekend were originally scrapped in favor of telerallies last week, although coverage of the cancellations apparently irked Trump enough to reinstate them.
 The president insisted last week that the telerally format is successful for him, saying they “only seem to work” for him because people tune in to hear him speak.

 False claims swirl after power outage briefly shuts down two voting sites near Phoenix
 By Marshall Cohen 
 Severe flooding and power outages briefly knocked out a couple of early voting sites near Phoenix on Monday – and quickly led to false claims of Democratic election shenanigans.
 Central Arizona saw major rainfall over the weekend , and two of the more than 50 early voting locations throughout Maricopa County lost power for a few hours on Monday.
 They were in a rural and conservative-leaning part of the county that includes Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, a competitive battleground in the fight for the US House.
 “It did take us a couple hours for the power company to get the power back on, and then for us to feel confident that we could advertise that the voting location would be open,” Maricopa County elections director Scott Jarrett said at a press conference Monday.
 The county declared an emergency over the floods. So did Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat running for re-election this year. That seemed to trigger the disinformation.
 Right-wing figures with millions of followers on social media claimed , without evidence, that this was part of a “stolen election” by Hobbs and unidentified Democrats who were trying to “pull games” with the results. Some even compared it to the 2020 election.
 A county official told CNN their office received hardly any calls from voters experiencing difficulties Monday. They also said the county uses “vote centers” where people can vote at any polling place, instead of their local precinct, alleviating issues from the outages.
 “A random Twitter account, just because it has a lot of followers, is not a reliable source of information,” the official said. “All measures are being taken to make sure our voters can vote.”

 Republicans tout $50 billion rural health fund, though their 2025 package slashes Medicaid
 By Tami Luhby 
 Republicans have been pointing to the billions of dollars their “big beautiful bill” will funnel into rural healthcare in an effort to counter the Democrats’ messaging that the bill’s sweeping Medicaid cuts will hurt rural hospitals and residents.
 In an op-ed in The Hill on Monday, GOP Rep. Harriet Hageman of Wyoming touted the $205 million that her state will receive from the Rural Health Transformation Program, which was added to the 2025 package at the last-minute to secure the votes of several holdout GOP senators. The program will “help address long-standing challenges specific to rural residents,” she wrote.
 Her colleague, Rep. Mike Kelly of Pennsylvania, praised the Trump administration for sending $35 million to the commonwealth for rural health needs.
 “Rural providers and hospitals are the backbone of our local health care communities,” Kelly said in an August statement. “This funding is a game changer for patients throughout the Commonwealth.”
 But the lawmakers don’t mention that the “big beautiful bill” also contains more than $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts , which are expected to hit rural hospitals and providers. Many of their patients depend on Medicaid for coverage. Plus, the rural funding cannot be used to make up funding losses from the bill’s other provisions.
 “If the Medicaid budget cuts go through, it’s going to be a disaster for access to healthcare for so many people across this country, particularly people who live in rural parts of the country,” Dr. Annie Andrews, who is running against GOP Sen. Darlene Graham of South Carolina, said on MS NOW on Saturday.

 In his final rally, Mike Rogers says he and Haley Stevens share one common thread
 By Taylor Romine 
 Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers speaks at an election eve event on November 2, in Rochester Hills, Michigan. 
 Paul Sancya/AP 
 While Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers and Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens might not have much in common politically, by the end of their brief conversation yesterday, Rogers was sure of one thing: They both “loved America.”
 Stevens has received blowback from Democrats for endorsing Rogers in the controversial Michigan Senate race after having a rocky relationship with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. But at Monday’s rally in Detroit, every mention of Stevens led to a burst of applause.
 “As soon as that church service was over, she leaned over and said, ‘I’m withdrawing my endorsement, and I’m endorsing you,’” Rogers said, recounting the moment from Sunday. “Listen, she probably didn’t agree with me on much on policy, but … we both knew that we both loved America, and we loved America more than we loved our parties.”
 Rogers spent most of the rally emphasizing that this race was about “the heart and soul of the country,” characterizing El-Sayed as a hateful person.
 “This election was never about how someone prayed, never. It was always about how you think and what your philosophy and what your ideology is,” Rogers said. “What it was about is that angry divisiveness that decided a certain segment of our society is the cause of all the ills in our community.”
 In some of his final words to the crowd, he said: “We’re going to be the Michigan that we grew up (in), and the Michigan that is great as it’s ever been.”

 Hillary Clinton tells CNN's Anderson Cooper Democrats should focus on affordability, corruption
 By Danya Gainor 
 Moving fast to address corruption concerns and affordability issues troubling Americans should be priority one for Democrats if they secure a majority in the House or Senate, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Monday.
 “The first bill will be about affordability, lowering costs, giving people the chance once again to afford healthcare,” Clinton said – then the party should prioritize battling corruption.
If Democrats gain a majority on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said he’d become “Mr. Veto ” in an effort to force Democrats to concede to him. 
“Lets get some (anti-corruption) legislation passed, and then go ahead and dare Trump to veto it,” said Clinton, who faced Trump in 2016 as the Democratic presidential nominee.

 Clinton says Stevens' endorsement of Rogers may help El-Sayed 
 0:58
 Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton doesn’t think Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ shocking break from her party to endorse Michigan’s GOP Senate candidate will have much impact on the outcome of the hotly contested race, she told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on the eve of the midterm election.
 “In fact, if it has any impact, I think that it will end up helping Abdul,” Clinton said of the Democratic candidate in the race, Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in a bitter primary battle over the summer.
 The race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers took a new turn this weekend when Stevens announced her last-minute endorsement of Rogers on Sunday morning but it’s unclear how much impact the move will have.
 CNN’s Poll of Polls average shows El-Sayed leading Rogers 50% to 45% and a recent CNN poll found 95% of Democratic likely voters backing the progressive.
 Clinton, Democrats’ 2016 presidential nominee, said she anticipates that voters will interpret the move as a “personal moment,” that is separate from “the issues that the people of Michigan actually want their candidates to talk about.”

 Ken Paxton says Texas Senate race is "about safeguarding our way of life"
 By Aditi Sangal 
 Ken Paxton, in his closing argument, said the Texas Senate midterms contest is “about defending our state and our country, but it’s also about safeguarding our way of life.”
 The GOP nominee touted his record as attorney general of the state and said his plan would put money in Texans’ pockets while his opponent James Talarico’s plan would take money from them.
 Paxton also painted Talarico as a “democratic socialist, just like AOC [Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez], just like New York Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani,” he told his supporters tonight in Allen, Texas.
 The Republican Texas Senate candidate ended by underscoring the importance of voting in this election.
 “Today, both sides have completely different objectives for this country. It isn’t just red vs. blue. It’s the America our founders gave us vs. something they would not recognize,” Paxton said. “The consequences will determine the future of Texas and America.”

 FBI expands investigation, visits Dan J. Sullivan donors in Alaska on election eve
 By Kyung Lah in Moose Pass, Alaska, and Curt Devine in Anchorage, Alaska
 On the eve of Election Day, the FBI investigation into the second Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s Senate race is expanding into multiple regions across the remote state.
 The FBI, which has flown agents to other remote areas of the state, has knocked on a dozen doors in Petersburg, Alaska, interviewing donors to Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent candidate on the ballot.
 “It’s unnerving that federal agents are chasing something like this down in the 11th hour ahead of Election Day,” said Jeigh Stanton Gregor, the vice mayor of Petersburg, who said two agents showed up at his doorstep and interviewed his wife Monday afternoon.
 The vice mayor of the community of 3,000 people told CNN that while the agents have been polite, they have been an alarming sight for the residents.
 “It feels a little authoritarian to send agents to investigate donors to a legitimate campaign,” Stanton Gregor said. “To go door to door to look for fraud? It makes me nervous this could happen in a free democracy and reeks of the DOJ interfering with politics.”
 He also called Daniel J. Sullivan, the political newcomer bearing nearly the identical name as Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a retired teacher and his friend.
 “Dan J. is our neighbor,” said Stanton Gregor, who donated $50. “To insinuate we’ve been confused in our donation, well, it’s laughable. There’s even a picture on his website. It’s comical.”
 Charles Flint, who also lives in Petersburg, said the FBI had been attempting to reach him, visiting both his former business, now run by his son, and his daughter’s residence a few days ago. Flint donated to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign, knowing him personally as a longtime customer of his business.
 Flint said he has not spoken directly to any agent.
 “I heard that Dan J. had thrown his hat in the ring … I thought, I can help the guy out. So I called him up and said, ‘Hey, I want to donate to your campaign. What’s your address?’” Flint said. “And he told me, and I sent him a check for $500.”
 The Petersburg resident expressed skepticism that there’s an obvious crime here, saying agents seemed to be “scratching away” to find a potential case.
 Mike Pilling of Juneau also said two FBI agents came to his house on Halloween. “We were hoping they were trick-or-treaters,” he said. Pilling said the agents indicated they were investigating whether there had been any fraud involved in political contributions to Daniel J Sullivan. Pilling said he told them he had indeed intended to contribute to the candidate.

 By Arlette Saenz and Jeff Simon in Portland, Maine
 Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson acknowledges supporters during a meet-and-greet at a bowling alley on the night before Election Day in Portland, Maine, on Tuesday. 
 Kevin Lamarque/Reuters 
 Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson rallied supporters at a bowling alley in Portland tonight, 100 days after securing the Democratic nomination arguing “It is our time.”
 “It’s not just about going back to where we were before Donald Trump, which would be a hell of a lot better than where we are right now,” Jackson said as he stood atop a bench at Bayside Bowl. “It’s about getting the government that you know Democrats should have been fighting for for a hell of a long time before this.”
 Jackson became the party’s nominee in July after Graham Platner exited the race following a string of controversies, including a sexual assault allegation he’s denied. He faces the GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins in the closely watched race that could determine control of the Senate.
 “I’ve waited so long for everyday people to rise up and demand a government that worked for them,” Jackson said. “I didn’t know I’d be standing here at Bayside Bowl in this position, but I am so honored to be with all of you.”
 Jackson bowled a few frames, drawing cheers after throwing a strike and picking up a spare.

 South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews arrives for a campaign event at The Refinery on Tuesday in Charleston, South Carolina.

 Democrat Annie Andrews wrapped her final rally tonight with a group singalong to “Happy Birthday” as her youngest child, Evelyn, blew out candles on a cake on stage to celebrate turning 10 years old.
 Hundreds of her supporters gathered in Charleston to close out what has been an unexpectedly competitive Senate campaign in a state that voted for President Donald Trump by nearly 18 points in 2024. 
 Andrews stuck to her usual stump speech, highlighting the price of gas, groceries and healthcare – with a special emphasis on that final issue, leaning on moments from her time as a pediatrician that she says inspired her to run for office.
 Andrews, who has cast herself as “an independent voice,” continued to make her case to frustrated Republicans, with thinly veiled shots at her opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill the remainder of her late brother’s Senate term in July before being asked by President Donald Trump to run for this full six-year Senate term.
 Despite the digs on Graham, Andrews preached unity and cautious confidence that a Democrat could win in the Palmetto State, as she imagined what Election night look like when the race is called.
 “The eyes of the nation will be on us.  Bayh hopes "change election" in Middle America will reverse Democrats’ fortunes in Indiana
 By Eric Bradner in Indianapolis
 Democratic candidate Beau Bayh listens during a secretary of state debate against Republican candidate Max Engling in Indianapolis on October 22. 
 Grace Smith/IndyStar/USA Today Network/Reuters 
 As Democrats look for a revival across the Rust Belt and Great Plains on Tuesday, Indiana might be the biggest reach of all. But Beau Bayh, the 30-year-old son and grandson of senators from bygone political eras in the barn-red state, says he believes a “change election” will break the GOP’s complete hold on the state’s government.
 Bayh is running for Indiana secretary of state. He is vying to become the first Democrat to win statewide in 14 years.
 In an interview after an election eve rally at a union hall in Indianapolis, he said the chances for a Democratic resurgence in states like Kansas, Iowa and Ohio are driven primarily by the economic fallout of President Donald Trump’s actions, including high diesel prices, hitting the region hardest.
 “It doesn’t matter what political party you’re in. Everyone pays for gas. Everyone pays for groceries. Everyone needs good health care. And all of those things have gone up,” he said. “What we’re hoping to see in this race is, people are fed up with the status quo, and they want a change. That’s what I think you are going to see tomorrow.”
 Nervous Democrats in the state said they believe Bayh can beat Republican Max Engling and two third-party candidates, and they think they have a shot at ousting GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz in the 5th Congressional District. But here, memories of 2018 — when the party lost a Senate seat in a Democratic wave election — are still fresh, and several long-time Democratic stalwarts said they were trying not to get their hopes up.
 Bayh is the grandson of one of the nation’s preeminent liberals, the late Sen. Birch Bayh. And he is the son of a well-known moderate, Evan Bayh, the former governor and senator.
 But a Midwestern politician whose approach he says he admires is Iowa state auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor.
 “He speaks to the frustration a lot of Americans have with the duopoly of our politics — something I actually agree with him on,” Bayh said of Sand, the lone Democrat to retain a statewide office in Iowa in a decade dominated by Trump. “It’s speaking to frustrations that people have with this two-party choice that they don’t like.”

 How Haley Stevens' endorsement unleashed simmering Democratic frustration at her fiancé
 By Eric Bradner , Patrick Svitek and Sarah Ferris 
 Rep. Haley Stevens, left, and her fiancé, Jason Turkish, right, stand with Senate candidate Mike Rogers and his wife, Kristi, during a church service Sunday in Detroit. 
 Jose Juarez/AP 
 Haley Stevens’ decision to drop her post-primary endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed and instead back Republican Mike Rogers for Senate has uncorked simmering Democratic anger at her fiancé , who told reporters he was voting for Rogers days before Stevens did so.
 Jason Turkish, a lawyer and donor, became Stevens’ fiancé this spring. A half-dozen sources who worked on Stevens’ Senate campaign and in her congressional office said in interviews Turkish had poor political instincts and little understanding of how campaigns operate.
 Stevens insists Turkish had nothing to do with her decision to endorse Rogers. In an interview on conservative commentator and CNN senior political contributor Scott Jennings’ radio show Monday, Stevens blamed talk of his influence on misogyny faced by female politicians and candidates.
 Turkish made more than $200,000 in federal contributions this election cycle. Many of those donations have gone to Michigan Democrats, but he’s also given to Sen. John Fetterman, a Pennsylvania Democrat who is a staunch Israel ally, as well as Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, another Israel supporter.
 In the radio interview, Turkish described himself as a “lifelong Democrat.”
 “Democratic politics is how I met the love of my life,” Turkish said. “I’m just not on board this one time.”
 Turkish has not been far from Stevens’ side in recent appearances. He joined her in the pew Sunday at a Detroit church where she first appeared with Rogers. And he was standing just offscreen last month when Stevens stopped by TMZ’s headquarters in Los Angeles.
